scope.scopeNotesMd: This report compares the base `Person` resource StructureDefinition in FHIR R4 4.0.1 with the `Person` resource in the local R6 6.0.0-ballot4 core package. The R6 artifact exists at the expected canonical path and keeps the same canonical URL, resource type, kind, base definition, derivation, and abstract flag. Findings are limited to local `Person` element, flag, order, cardinality, binding, and semantic-text changes. Changes inherited only from `Resource`, `DomainResource`, `Element`, or `BackboneElement` are explicitly excluded from `findings[]` under the inherited/base-artifact rule.
outOfScope: Inherited `Resource` and `DomainResource` changes on `Person.id`, `Person.meta`, `Person.implicitRules`, `Person.language`, `Person.text`, `Person.contained`, `Person.extension`, and `Person.modifierExtension`, including the Resource.language binding change from preferred common languages to required all-languages.

Inherited `Element` and `BackboneElement` child changes on `Person.link.id`, `Person.link.extension`, `Person.link.modifierExtension`, and the corresponding inherited children under the new `Person.communication` backbone.
Base invariant text or expression changes sourced from `Element`, `Resource`, or `DomainResource`, including `ele-1` and `dom-*` constraint evolution.

Search parameters, operations, CapabilityStatement behavior, implementation-guide profiles, examples outside the two core package directories, and changes in referenced resources such as Patient, Practitioner, RelatedPerson, and Organization.
General R6 ballot package publication status and infrastructure changes except where the local Person StructureDefinition identity is directly relevant.

narrativeReportMd:
# Person R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No local `Person` element was removed and no local mandatory element was added, so most ordinary R4 JSON `Person` instances remain structurally acceptable in R6. The main breaking concern is a **potential XML/order break**: `Person.active` moved much earlier in the resource sequence. The main migration risk is in the opposite direction: R6 adds `deceased[x]`, `maritalStatus`, and `communication`, and allows multiple `photo` values, none of which can be represented cleanly in base R4 without extensions, truncation, or policy-specific transforms.

## Scope
The report analyzes local `Person` differences only. Inherited changes from `Resource`, `DomainResource`, `Element`, and `BackboneElement` are out of scope, including the inherited `Resource.language` binding change and base invariant changes.

## Main migration themes
The R6 resource is broader and more expressive: it can carry death status/date, marital status, communication language preferences, and multiple photos. These are not R4-to-R6 validation breaks because they are optional or widening changes, but they are important for R6-to-R4 exchange and code generation. R6 also changes summary behavior for `identifier` and `address`, which can affect `_summary` responses and privacy review.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact findings are `Person:SERIALIZATION_OR_CODEGEN:active-order:a7b0c1` for XML element order and the R6-only data findings for `deceased[x]`, `maritalStatus`, `communication`, and widened `photo`.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important when deciding how to down-convert R6 death status, marital status, communication preferences, and multiple photos to R4. A project may choose official or local extensions, loss-aware truncation, profile-specific preservation, or rejection of non-representable R6 content.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Most R6 additions are reasonable optional model growth, but they would have been easier to exchange with R4 systems if paired with explicit cross-version extensions and conversion maps. The `active` order move appears more avoidable because preserving existing element order and only inserting new optional elements would have reduced XML compatibility risk.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `Person` keeps the same identity and has no local removals or required additions, but R6 changes XML/codegen order for `active`, adds several R6-only optional data elements, widens `photo`, and changes summary behavior for `identifier` and `address`. The top migration concerns are XML sequence compatibility, R6-to-R4 data loss for new elements, and privacy/behavior changes in summary responses. Confidence is high for computable structural deltas; official narrative diffs and conversion maps would improve confidence on intent and recommended transforms.
summary.migrationThemesMd: For R4-to-R6, check XML serializers and validators for `Person.active` order and review code generated from ordered element lists. For R6-to-R4, decide how to preserve or reject `deceased[x]`, `maritalStatus`, `communication`, and multiple `photo` values. For runtime behavior, audit `_summary` handling and any identity-management logic that used `telecom` rather than identifiers.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for local StructureDefinition changes because both assigned StructureDefinitions were present and directly compared. Confidence is medium for clinical or workflow impact because the official rendered specification pages, ballot change notes, and conversion ConceptMaps were not available. Terminology confidence is high for the unchanged administrative-gender and identity-assurance code sets inspected locally, but lower for open-ended BCP-47 language expansion behavior.

findings.title: Person.active moved earlier in the resource element sequence

oldState.summary: `Person.active` appeared late in the local R4 Person sequence, after `Person.managingOrganization` and before `Person.link`.
oldState.narrativeMd: In R4 the local child order placed `active` after `managingOrganization`. R4 XML serializers commonly emit elements in this StructureDefinition order.

newState.summary: `Person.active` appears immediately after `Person.identifier` and before `Person.name` in the R6 local sequence.
newState.narrativeMd: In R6 the same `active` element is still optional, boolean, modifier, and summary, but its ordered position is much earlier in `Person`.

facts.note: Only local Person children are shown; inherited Resource/DomainResource children are omitted.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element id and path are unchanged (`Person.active`), so this is a sequence move rather than a rename.

impact.impactRationaleMd: FHIR JSON member order is not significant, so JSON instances are not affected by this change. FHIR XML serialization is order-sensitive in many schema/validator and generated-parser paths. An R4 XML instance emitted in R4 order with `<active>` after `<managingOrganization>` can be rejected or require reordering when validated as R6; an R6 XML instance with `<active>` near the top can similarly surprise R4 XML tooling.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The risk is primarily technical interoperability. `active` is a modifier, so parsers that miss it due to ordering assumptions could also make unsafe assumptions about record usability, but conformant parsers should not ignore parse errors.

justification.inferredGoal: Align Person's element order with related demographic resources or place the modifier/status field earlier for visibility.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Preserve the R4 position of Person.active and insert optional new R6 elements without moving existing children.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of placing the active/status modifier earlier is reasonable, but the changed order creates XML sequence and generated-code churn for an otherwise unchanged element. The supplied evidence does not show that R6 needed to move `Person.active` to add the new optional elements or clarify its semantics, so this level of breakage looks avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base R6 design could have kept `Person.active` after `Person.managingOrganization` as in R4 and inserted the new optional R6 elements without reordering existing children. That would preserve R4-valid XML ordering and old generated property order while still supporting `deceased[x]`, `maritalStatus`, `communication`, and other R6 model growth. The tradeoff is less harmonized ordering if other demographic resources place active/status fields near identifiers.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Stable ordering preserves XML and generated-code compatibility; moving active earlier may improve status visibility and harmonization with related models.

evidence.detail: R4 sequence places Person.active after Person.managingOrganization and before Person.link.
R6 sequence places Person.active after Person.identifier and before Person.name.

examples.examplesMd: Illustrative XML issue: an R4-ordered XML `Person` that emits `<managingOrganization/>` before `<active/>` follows the R4 StructureDefinition order but not the R6 local order. JSON examples are not useful because JSON property order is not semantically significant.

findings.narrativeMd: `Person.active` did not change its path, type, cardinality, modifier flag, or summary flag, but it moved from late in the resource to immediately after `identifier`. This matters mainly for XML and generated code that treats StructureDefinition order as the canonical serialization sequence. It is not a data-content break for JSON, but it can be a strict XML validation or parser break for otherwise valid R4 instances.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 JSON instances remain compatible with respect to `active`. R4 XML instances that contain `active` in R4 order may need reserialization to satisfy R6 order. R6 XML instances containing `active` in the R6 position may not validate as R4 XML. This is a serialization/order compatibility issue rather than a semantic value-domain change.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Regenerate serializers from the R6 definitions and include XML round-trip tests with `active` present. R4-to-R6 migration should parse and re-emit XML rather than textually copying element order. Code generators should avoid treating the old property order as stable.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because the same element could have been left in place, this order move appears likely avoidable from a compatibility perspective. If the goal was harmonization with other resources, the tradeoff is improved consistency at the cost of XML sequence compatibility.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confirm against the official R6 XML schema or validator behavior if XML compatibility is a priority. Some FHIR parsers may accept out-of-order XML and normalize internally, which would reduce practical impact.

findings.title: R6 adds optional Person.deceased[x] with boolean and dateTime choices

oldState.summary: R4 Person had no local death-status or death-date element.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 systems could only represent this information using extensions or linked resources; there was no base `Person.deceased[x]` element.

newState.summary: R6 Person has optional `deceased[x]` with boolean and dateTime choices.

semanticText.short: Indicates if the individual is deceased or not
semanticText.definition: Indicates if the individual is deceased or not.
semanticText.comment: If there's no value in the instance, it means there is no statement on whether or not the individual is deceased. Most systems will interpret the absence of a value as a sign of the person being alive.

newState.narrativeMd: The new element supports either a boolean deceased indicator or a dateTime of death and is included in R6 summaries.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not an R4-to-R6 validation break because the new element is optional. It is a high R6-to-R4 representability risk: base R4 `Person` has no corresponding element, so death status or death date is lost unless mapped to an extension or external resource. Strict R4 parsers will reject `deceasedBoolean` or `deceasedDateTime` when an R6 instance is treated as R4.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Death status can affect identity matching, outreach, consent, and administrative workflows. Loss during down-conversion could cause inappropriate communication or record-use decisions.

justification.inferredGoal: Represent whether a person is deceased directly on the context-independent Person record.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: this is optional R6 content that preserves R4-to-R6 base instance validity.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of representing deceased status or date directly on `Person` is reasonable for demographic and administrative use. Because `Person.deceased[x]` is optional, existing R4 instances are not made invalid in R6; the material risk is loss or rejection when R6 content is projected back into R4.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: No backward-compatible base-design alternative is applicable for the R4-to-R6 direction because the addition itself is optional. Publishing an R4 extension, cross-version map, or conversion rule would be important interoperability mitigation for R6-to-R4 exchange, but those are not less-breaking R6 base designs. Omitting the element from base R6 would avoid down-conversion pressure but would not meet the goal of native R6 representation.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6 gains native deceased status/date support; mixed-version exchange still needs extension or conversion policy, which is mitigation rather than a base-design alternative.

evidence.detail: No element with id `Person.deceased[x]` exists in the R4 Person snapshot.
R6 adds `Person.deceased[x]` with cardinality 0..1, types boolean and dateTime, and isSummary true.

examples.examplesMd: The example is an illustrative fragment. The `deceasedDateTime` property is valid R6 shape for the new choice element but has no base R4 `Person` counterpart.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds a direct death-status/death-date element to `Person`. Existing R4 data is not invalidated, but systems that move R6 `Person` records back to R4 must decide how to preserve the information. Treating the R6 instance as R4 without conversion will either fail strict validation or drop clinically and administratively meaningful data.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6: no hard validation break because absence remains allowed. R6-to-R4: a valid R6 instance with `deceasedBoolean` or `deceasedDateTime` is not representable in base R4. Generated R4 classes and JSON/XML schema validators will not have a property for the new choice element.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For down-conversion, use a project-approved extension or retain the R6 payload alongside the R4 projection. Test boolean and dateTime choices separately, including partial dateTime precision and absence semantics. Avoid silently interpreting absence as alive if the migration dropped an explicit death value.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 addition is optional and therefore mostly backward-compatible in the forward direction. The missing piece is a standard R4 preservation path; an official extension and ConceptMap-like conversion rule would make the change less disruptive for mixed-version ecosystems.

findings.title: R6 adds optional Person.maritalStatus

oldState.summary: R4 Person had no base marital-status element.
oldState.narrativeMd: Marital status could not be represented directly on base R4 `Person`.

newState.summary: R6 Person adds optional `maritalStatus` as CodeableConcept with an extensible marital-status binding.

binding.description: The domestic partnership status of a person.

semanticText.definition: This field contains a person's most recent marital (civil) status.
semanticText.comment: Many countries maintain a register of births, deaths and marriages, and this would simplify that interaction

newState.narrativeMd: The new element carries civil/domestic partnership status and binds extensibly to the marital-status value set.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The element is optional, so existing R4 instances remain valid with respect to this addition. A valid R6 instance carrying marital status has no base R4 location, and strict R4 parsers will reject the unknown `maritalStatus` member. Because the binding is extensible, local codes may also require policy review during conversion.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Marital or domestic-partnership status may drive administrative, legal, consent, or next-of-kin workflows depending on jurisdiction.

justification.inferredGoal: Support civil status on generic person records, harmonizing with common demographic models.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: an optional R6 maritalStatus element does not create a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of supporting civil or domestic-partnership status on a generic person record is plausible, and the element is optional with unchanged validity for R4 instances that omit it. The compatibility concern is principally reverse exchange and terminology policy for R6 data, not forward R4-to-R6 invalidation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A standard R4 extension or conversion map can reduce data loss when sending R6 `maritalStatus` to R4 systems, but that is a backport/mitigation path rather than a base R6 design alternative. Keeping marital status out of base R6 would be less expressive and would not satisfy the goal of making the concept discoverable in the R6 Person model.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6 improves native civil-status modeling; R6-to-R4 preservation requires extensions or policy-specific conversion, not a less-breaking base R6 alternative.

evidence.detail: No `Person.maritalStatus` element exists in the R4 Person snapshot.
R6 adds `Person.maritalStatus` 0..1 CodeableConcept with extensible binding to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/marital-status`.
The local R4 and R6 value sets both include v3-MaritalStatus and NullFlavor UNK in compose, though the element itself is new on Person in R6.

examples.examplesMd: The fragment shows R6 content with no base R4 `Person` property. An R4 extension or separate administrative record would be needed to preserve it.

findings.narrativeMd: `Person.maritalStatus` is a new optional civil-status field. It does not invalidate R4 instances, but it creates a clear R6-to-R4 data-loss point because base R4 `Person` has no equivalent element.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is unaffected when the element is absent. R6-to-R4 validation fails for strict R4 schemas or generated classes if `maritalStatus` is present. A lossy transform that drops the field can change administrative or legal semantics.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Define a down-conversion strategy: map to a standard/local extension, preserve the original R6 resource, or reject records where marital status must not be lost. Include tests for value-set codes, NullFlavor `UNK`, local codings, and text-only CodeableConcept values.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The optional addition is forward-compatible, but the same information could have been introduced with an explicit R4 extension and official conversion guidance to reduce mixed-version disruption. The tradeoff is more extension reliance in R4 implementations.

findings.title: R6 adds Person.communication backbone for language communication preferences

oldState.summary: R4 Person had no local communication-language backbone.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `Person` could not directly carry communication language or language preference as base elements.

newState.summary: R6 adds repeatable `communication` with required `language` and optional `preferred`.

semanticText.short: A language which may be used to communicate with the person about his or her health
semanticText.definition: A language which may be used to communicate with the person about his or her health.

newState.narrativeMd: Each R6 communication entry requires `communication.language` (1..1 CodeableConcept, required binding to all-languages) and may include `communication.preferred` (0..1 boolean).

impact.impactRationaleMd: The parent is optional, so R4 instances do not become invalid in R6. But if R6 uses `communication`, a base R4 `Person` cannot carry the language/preference structure. The nested required `language` is not an R4-to-R6 problem because it applies only when a new communication entry exists; it is a validation rule R6 producers must satisfy.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Communication language and interpreter needs can affect patient-facing communication, consent, and safety. Loss during down-conversion may route communication in the wrong language.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow Person to record languages that can be used for health communication and preference among them.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the new communication backbone is optional, so old R4 Person instances remain valid in R6.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of recording communication languages and preferences on `Person` is reasonable and follows a common demographic pattern. The required `communication.language` child applies only when a new R6 communication entry is present, so it does not make existing R4 instances invalid.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: For R4-to-R6 compatibility, no less-breaking base R6 alternative is needed because the backbone is optional. R4 extensions or mappings to linked Patient, Practitioner, or RelatedPerson resources can help preserve R6 data during down-conversion, but those are mitigations and may be semantically unsafe without context. Omitting the R6 backbone would avoid reverse-version data loss but would not meet the native R6 modeling goal.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6 gains native language-preference structure; R6-to-R4 conversion still needs an extension or carefully scoped role-resource mapping.

evidence.detail: No `Person.communication` element exists in the R4 Person snapshot.
R6 requires `Person.communication.language` 1..1 CodeableConcept bound required to all-languages with common languages as starter binding.

examples.examplesMd: This R6 fragment has no base R4 `Person` location. Mapping it to a linked `Patient.communication` may be wrong unless the linked patient role and consent/workflow context are known.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds a repeatable communication-language backbone to `Person`. It is optional for the resource as a whole, but each communication entry must include a language. The addition is useful but creates a non-trivial down-conversion problem because the R4 `Person` model has no equivalent structure and linked role resources are not always semantically interchangeable.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6: no break unless a system creates an R6 communication entry without the required language. R6-to-R4: strict R4 parsers reject `communication`, and lossy transforms drop language preference. The language binding is required in R6 but open-ended through BCP-47, so validation depends on language-tag handling rather than a small finite code list.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Use a standard or local extension for R4 preservation, or define role-specific mapping rules only when it is safe to copy communication preferences to linked Patient/Practitioner/RelatedPerson resources. Test multiple communication entries, preferred flags, text-only CodeableConcepts, and BCP-47 regional tags.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: An optional R6 backbone is forward-compatible for old data. A companion R4 extension and conversion map would make it much safer for mixed-version exchange. Automatic mapping to linked resources is only a partial alternative because R6 comments warn against updating linked practitioner resources from this property without context.

findings.title: Person.photo maximum cardinality widened from 1 to *

oldState.summary: R4 allowed at most one photo.

newState.summary: R6 allows zero or more photos.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 keeps the same type and definition but permits multiple `Attachment` values.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Increasing max cardinality is not an R4-to-R6 validation break; every R4-valid cardinality remains allowed. It is a high R6-to-R4 risk when more than one photo is present because R4 permits only one. Codegen also changes from a singleton property in R4-oriented models to a collection in R6-oriented models.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Multiple photos mainly affect identification and display. Loss of additional photos is usually lower risk than loss of status or language data, but may matter for identity matching or fraud-prevention workflows.

justification.inferredGoal: Support multiple images for a person, such as current and alternate identification photos.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: widening Person.photo from 0..1 to 0..* preserves R4-valid instance content in R6.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Supporting multiple person photos is a plausible model improvement, and the cardinality widening does not invalidate R4 instances with zero or one photo. The remaining disruption is generated-model shape change and inability to represent multiple R6 photos in base R4, not a forward validation break.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Because this is a widening that preserves old instance cardinalities, a backward-compatible alternative is not applicable in the R4-to-R6 base-design sense. A design that kept `photo` singleton and added a separate additional-photo field would reduce generated API churn but introduce duplicate same-resource representations and ambiguity about primary versus additional photos. R4 extensions or truncation rules are down-conversion mitigations, not reasons to classify an R6 base alternative as available.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6 supports multiple photos natively; R4 down-conversion and generated API shape changes still need explicit handling.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example is illustrative and uses a placeholder extension URL; projects should use an approved extension if available.

findings.narrativeMd: `Person.photo` changed from a singleton to a repeatable element. This is safe for old R4 content moving forward, but R6 content with multiple photos cannot be faithfully represented in base R4. Generated classes and serializers may also change API shape from an optional attachment to a list.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6: no cardinality validation break. R6-to-R4: a Person with two or more photos violates R4 `0..1` cardinality unless extra photos are dropped or moved to extensions/related resources. XML and JSON validators should both enforce this cardinality difference.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Down-conversion should define a deterministic primary-photo selection rule and a preservation strategy for additional photos. Test zero, one, and multiple photos. Avoid silent truncation unless business owners accept the loss.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is a classic widening: easy for forward compatibility, risky for reverse compatibility. A separate extension for extra photos would have preserved R4 shape but made R6's base support less straightforward.

findings.title: Person.identifier and Person.address are newly included in summaries

oldState.summary: R4 did not mark `Person.identifier` or `Person.address` as summary elements.
oldState.narrativeMd: In the R4 snapshot both local elements have `isSummary` false.

newState.summary: R6 marks both `Person.identifier` and `Person.address` as summary elements.
newState.narrativeMd: In the R6 snapshot both elements have `isSummary` true. Their cardinalities and datatypes remain unchanged.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Summary flags do not affect base instance validity. They can affect server `_summary` responses, generated summary serializers, indexing, and privacy assumptions. R6 summary views may include identifiers and addresses that R4 summary consumers did not receive or expect.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Identifiers and addresses are sensitive demographic data. Including them in summary representations can change privacy exposure and payload size.

justification.inferredGoal: Make key identifying demographics available in summary/search-result representations.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the base summary flags unchanged and rely on _elements, profiles, or implementation-guide summary rules for clients that need identifier and address.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of making identifiers and addresses available in summary representations is reasonable for matching and display, but it changes runtime and privacy expectations for systems that derive summaries from `isSummary`. A less-breaking approach exists, though it would not deliver the same uniform default summary behavior across base R6 systems.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A partially backward-compatible base design would leave `Person.identifier` and `Person.address` out of the base summary set and direct clients to request them with `_elements` or profiles where needed. That preserves R4-era summary payload expectations and reduces accidental exposure of sensitive demographics. The tradeoff is material: clients cannot rely on base `_summary=true` to include key matching fields, and implementations may fragment through local summary conventions.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This preserves old summary/privacy expectations but weakens default R6 summary usefulness and creates more opt-in variability.

evidence.detail: R4 snapshot marks both elements as not summary.
R6 snapshot marks both elements as summary.

examples.examplesMd: A server that derives `_summary=true` from `isSummary` may begin returning `identifier` and `address` in summary bundles after upgrading definitions. This is not an instance-validation example.

findings.narrativeMd: Two sensitive demographic fields moved into the summary set. This does not make any instance invalid and does not create a new data element, but it can change API behavior for clients, caches, generated summary models, and privacy reviews.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: FHIR validators should not reject instances because of this flag change. The compatibility mechanism is runtime behavior: summary serialization and query responses may contain additional fields. R4-to-R6 and R6-to-R4 structural representability are not the issue.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Audit summary/search-result APIs, generated summary projections, logging, caching, and privacy rules. Add regression tests for `_summary=true` or equivalent server behavior if it is driven by StructureDefinition metadata.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been avoided by leaving summary flags unchanged and relying on `_elements` for clients that need identifiers or addresses. The tradeoff is that Person summaries would be less useful for matching and display.

findings.title: R6 adds user-identity guidance: use identifier, not telecom

oldState.summary: R4 had no local comment directing user identities to `identifier` or away from `telecom`.

semanticText.comment: R4 `Person.telecom` comment described contact methods; R4 `Person.identifier` had no user-identity guidance.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 described `telecom` as contact details and `identifier` as identifiers, without explicit guidance about login/user identities.

newState.summary: R6 says systems may use `identifier` for user identities using type `USER` and says not to use `.telecom` properties to represent user identities.

semanticText.comment: Systems MAY use identifier for user identities (using the type='USER'). DO NOT use .telecom properties to represent user identities.

newState.narrativeMd: The R6 comments introduce a semantic/conformance expectation for identity representation while leaving both elements structurally unchanged.

facts.newValue: Systems MAY use identifier for user identities (using the type='USER').

facts.oldValue: Contact details only; no user identity warning.
facts.newValue: DO NOT use .telecom properties to represent user identities.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not enforced by cardinality, type, or binding in the base StructureDefinition, so validators generally will not reject an instance solely for having user-like values in `telecom`. It is still a conformance and business-rule change: systems that used email/phone telecom values as login identities may need to model those identities as identifiers with type `USER` in R6.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Identity representation affects authentication, user linking, audit, and privacy. Misusing contact points as user identities can create account-linking or duplicate-identity risks.

justification.inferredGoal: Separate contact details from system/user identity identifiers for security and privacy clarity.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking base design was identified; R6 already uses non-validating guidance rather than structural constraints.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Separating contact points from user identities is a reasonable security and privacy goal. R6 implements that goal with comments and guidance instead of changing cardinality, type, binding, or adding a hard invariant, so old instances generally remain valid even if implementations need semantic review.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The current design is already close to the least disruptive base approach: it warns against using `telecom` for user identities and points implementers toward `identifier` without making validators reject existing contact points. Keeping the R4 text unchanged would be less disruptive only by failing the R6 clarification goal, while a hard invariant or required migration to `identifier` would be substantially more breaking.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Omitting or weakening the guidance preserves ambiguous R4 practice but fails the security/privacy clarification; enforcing it structurally would be more breaking.

evidence.detail: R4 lacks user-identity guidance on identifier and does not warn against representing user identities in telecom.
R6 adds identifier guidance for type `USER` and a `DO NOT use .telecom properties to represent user identities` warning.

examples.examplesMd: The example is illustrative: the same email-like string may remain as a contact point, but user-account identity should be represented as an identifier when that is the intended meaning.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 draws a clearer line between contact details and user identities. This can surprise systems that used `Person.telecom` as a convenient login-name or account-identifier field. The data shape still validates, but conformance review and security logic may need to change.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is generally still-valid-but-behaviorally-different, not old-valid/new-invalid. Base validators do not know whether a telecom value is being used as a user identity. The compatibility mechanism is business logic, profile conformance, and security/privacy review rather than JSON/XML schema validation.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory uses of `Person.telecom` in authentication, account-linking, and user provisioning flows. Where a telecom value functions as a user identity, add or migrate to `Person.identifier` with an appropriate user-identity type and keep `telecom` only for contact semantics. Test duplicate-account and audit workflows.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: R6 chose a relatively backward-compatible path by adding guidance rather than a hard invariant. Stronger validation would be difficult and likely over-reject legitimate contact details. Profiles can enforce stricter local rules where necessary.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: Canonical URL, id/name/type `Person`, kind `resource`, abstract flag `false`, baseDefinition `DomainResource`, and specialization derivation are unchanged. The artifact was not renamed, split, merged, or removed.
No local R4 Person element was removed or renamed. R6 additions are reported as findings; inherited base children are out of scope.
No local minimum cardinality increased and no local maximum cardinality decreased. The only local cardinality change found is the widening of `Person.photo`, reported separately.
No type was removed or narrowed on common local elements. New R6 element types for `deceased[x]`, `maritalStatus`, and `communication` are reported separately.

`Person.managingOrganization` remains `Reference(Organization)`. `Person.link.target` retains the same target profiles: Patient, Practitioner, RelatedPerson, and Person. The R6 type includes a hierarchy extension, but the target set is unchanged.

Local existing required bindings for `Person.gender` and `Person.link.assurance` still point to the same canonical value sets with version updates. Local code-system inspection found the same administrative-gender codes and the same identity-assurance codes. New bindings for added elements are covered in findings. The inherited `Resource.language` binding change is out of scope.
No new local Person-specific invariant was identified on existing local elements. Constraint text/expression changes sourced from base `Element` or `DomainResource` are inherited and excluded.
No local fixed value, pattern, or default value constraints were found to be added, removed, or changed for Person.
No local maxLength, regex, minValue, or maxValue restrictions were found to be added or tightened for Person.
`Person.active` remains the only local modifier element and its modifier reason is unchanged. Inherited modifierExtension changes are out of scope.
No local slicing discriminator, ordering, or slicing rule changes were found for Person.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Person advances from draft/trial-use FMM 2 to active/normative FMM 4 metadata
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Artifact maturity/status metadata does not by itself make instances valid or invalid. It does, however, signal a more stable R6 resource definition and may affect governance expectations.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Treat this as a planning signal: R6 `Person` may have stronger stability expectations even though the package is a ballot build marked not for publication.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 explicitly records mustSupport=false on many Person elements
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: An explicit `mustSupport: false` is not a strengthening over an absent mustSupport flag in the base StructureDefinition. It should not create validation failures.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Code generators or metadata diff tools should normalize absent and false mustSupport values to avoid noisy false positives.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Existing required bindings are version-updated but code sets inspected locally are unchanged
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: `Person.gender` and `Person.link.assurance` still bind required to their respective value sets; local CodeSystem comparison found the same codes and definitions for administrative gender and identity assurance levels.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology validators should load the R6 package versions, but existing R4 codes `male`, `female`, `other`, `unknown`, and `level1`-`level4` remain valid based on local package contents.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Several visible snapshot changes on inherited Person elements come from `Resource` or `DomainResource`, including `Resource.language` binding changes, contained-resource text, summary behavior for inherited modifierExtension, and dom-* invariant expression updates. These should be owned by the base resource reports, not this Person report.
Changes on inherited `id`, `extension`, `modifierExtension`, and `ele-1` constraints under `Person.link` and `Person.communication` belong to Element/BackboneElement analysis.

Lossless down-conversion of R6-only `Person` content (`deceased[x]`, `maritalStatus`, `communication`, and multiple photos) needs official or project-specific conversion mappings and extension choices.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The analysis did not include an official HL7 R4-to-R6 Person diff or ballot change rationale, so justification assessments are inferred from StructureDefinition content.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Compare against the official rendered diff or ballot change notes for `Person`.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Terminology comparison used local ValueSet/CodeSystem compose and concept content only. No live expansion was performed for open-ended BCP-47 language tags or external terminology packages.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run terminology expansion with the intended R4 and R6 terminology servers and compare expansions for value sets used by Person.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The XML/order finding is based on StructureDefinition order and normal FHIR XML ordering expectations; this report did not run sample XML through official R4 and R6 validators or schemas.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Validate R4-ordered and R6-ordered sample XML with official FHIR validators configured for R4 and R6 ballot packages.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official conversion ConceptMap or cross-version extension catalog was used to determine preferred transforms for R6-only Person elements.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Use official HL7 cross-version maps or approved project mappings for Person.
